theme: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 118. This is the last of the Hallel psalms, which Jews sang at Passover. It was likely sung by Jesus and the disciples on the night of the Last Supper. Read it as the psalm of the week you have just entered.
settingTheScene: Psalm 118 is a thanksgiving liturgy for a king who has been delivered. Verses 22 to 29 were part of what the crowds shouted on Palm Sunday. Jesus quoted it in the parable of the tenants. The Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118) was sung at Passover, which makes it very likely that this was the last hymn Jesus sang before Gethsemane (Matthew 26:30).
observation: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
“Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free” (v. 5).
“The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (v. 6).
“It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man” (v. 8).
“The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation” (v. 14).
“I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD” (v. 17).
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (v. 22).
“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!” (v. 26).
interpretation:
The psalm begins and ends with the same refrain: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good.” Between those lines, a man who has been surrounded and nearly killed tells how God rescued him. “All nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off!” He was pushed hard, but the LORD helped him. “The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.”

Then he asks to enter the gates of righteousness to give thanks, and the main verses follow. The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. In the original setting, it probably referred to Israel, once despised by the nations, or to the Davidic king. In the New Testament it is applied to Jesus. The builders, the leaders of Israel, rejected him, and God made him the cornerstone of the new temple.

Then the crowd’s words: “Save us, we pray, O LORD!” (Hosanna) and “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!” On Palm Sunday, the crowd shouted these words to Jesus. They did not yet understand how he would save. The one who comes in the LORD’s name would enter the gates of Jerusalem and go to a cross.

Think about Jesus singing this psalm on the night he was betrayed. “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear.” “I shall not die, but I shall live.” “Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar!” The psalm of the rejected stone was sung by the rejected stone, on his way to be rejected.

And it ends with praise. “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you.” The cross is not the end.
connection: Matthew 21:9, 21:42, and 23:39 quote this psalm. Matthew 26:30 says that after singing a hymn they went out to the Mount of Olives. Acts 4:11-12 and 1 Peter 2:6-8 apply the cornerstone to Jesus. Ephesians 2:20-22 describes the household of God built on the cornerstone. Romans 8:31: if God is for us, who can be against us? Hebrews 13:6 quotes verse 6. Hebrews 12:2.
application:
Sing or read Psalm 118:1 and 29 as a frame for your day. Begin and end with thanks.

Remember a time when God brought you out of distress. Tell someone about it.

Pray verse 25, “Save us, we pray,” for your church and for someone who needs rescue.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for his steadfast love.
Tell him: “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear.”
Thank him for the stone the builders rejected.
